assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks combine laser cooling, magic-wavelength trapping and ultranarrow optical transitions into a clear, original invention that improved frequency-measurement accuracy and stability by orders of magnitude. The atomic-structure side (magic wavelengths, systematic shifts from blackbody radiation, hyperfine and higher-order light shifts) is exactly the kind of controlled atomic physics that has lasting consequences for the SI second, geodesy, tests of fundamental constants and searches for new physics.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and first demonstrated it; Ye led the group that pushed the clocks to the 10^-18 regime and developed the many-body (Fermi-degenerate) clock. Two laureates give a clean, defensible configuration. Other contributors (for example Lemonde, Hollberg, Lisdat or Ludlow-type work) are not in the credited list, and the relative weight of the scientific idea versus the engineering refinement is a judgement call.
assessment.maturity: Mature and independently confirmed by many laboratories worldwide, with clock comparisons below 10^-18 and active roadmaps toward a redefinition of the second. Hall and Hänsch (2005) already recognised the frequency-comb part, so the remaining clock contribution is distinct and timely.
uncertainties: Whether the committee prefers to wait for the formal redefinition of the second.
Overlap with the earlier ion-clock and frequency-comb prizes may be seen as incremental by some members.
I am relying on my own recollection of priority and have not verified details of the first demonstrations.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum simulation with ultracold atoms in optical lattices (the Mott-insulator transition, programmable Hubbard models, single-site-resolved quantum gas microscopes) opened a new way to study strongly correlated many-body physics with atomic-physics control. It is original, conceptually clear and has influenced condensed-matter, quantum-information and many-body theory.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch, Cirac and others) supplied the theoretical proposal for Hubbard physics in lattices; Greiner realised the Mott transition and the quantum gas microscope; Bloch led the broad experimental programme. Cirac's contribution is large but overlaps with the trapped-ion candidate, and the four-name list is too long for one prize. Jaksch is not on the list, which makes the theory-side credit imperfect.
assessment.maturity: Highly mature, reproduced in dozens of laboratories, with analogue simulators now reaching regimes beyond classical numerics. Recognition is timely, though the quantum-simulation field is still evolving.
uncertainties: The theory proposal (Jaksch et al., 1998) is not fully represented by the credited names.
Overlap of Cirac and Zoller with the trapped-ion and atomic quantum-information candidates complicates a coherent allocation.
Whether the committee sees the discovery as a method rather than a single discovery.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: A theoretical prediction of flat bands at a magic twist angle was followed by the experimental discovery of correlated insulators and superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene. It created the moire-materials field and a new, tunable platform for correlated and topological phases. It is a rare case where a clean prediction and a clean experiment link directly.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald made the key 2011 theoretical prediction; Jarillo-Herrero's group made the decisive 2018 experimental discovery. The three-person configuration looks natural. Cao and others in the experiment, and Santos and Peres (earlier twisted-bilayer theory), are not credited, which leaves some allocation tension.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed independently by multiple groups across several moire systems, though the origin of the superconducting pairing remains debated. The field is young for a prize, but the original discovery is well established.
uncertainties: The pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is still unresolved.
Priority issues around earlier theoretical work and the role of the first author of the experiment.
Possible prematurity compared with candidates with a longer track record.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: X-ray free-electron lasers (SASE concept, high-gain theory, realisation at LCLS, SACLA and European XFEL, plus the earlier FLASH) deliver femtosecond, intense, coherent X-ray pulses. They enable time-resolved studies of inner-shell and multiphoton processes in atoms, molecules and solids, and are central to ultrafast structural science. Impact is very large, and for atomic physics it is direct: core-hole dynamics and nonlinear X-ray processes.
assessment.attribution: Pellegrini and Kim are commonly credited for SASE theory and design; Rossbach for the FLASH/TESLA test facility and European XFEL. Others (Bonifacio, Saldin, Schneidmiller, Yurkov, Emma and the LCLS team) also made decisive contributions, so a three-person prize would be difficult to defend as complete.
assessment.maturity: Facilities are operating and widely used; the science output is substantial and independent. Recognition would be timely, but this is partly an accelerator-technology achievement and so sits at the edge of the Physics Prize tradition.
uncertainties: Credit among the SASE theorists and facility builders is contested.
Whether the prize should reward the machine concept or the science enabled.
My assessment of the relative contributions of the Saldin-Schneidmiller-Yurkov group versus the credited names is based on memory.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller proposal for ion-trap quantum gates, followed by experimental realisation of entangling gates, quantum algorithms and error-corrected operations with trapped ions, is a foundational element of quantum computing. It is original and conceptually clear, and trapped ions remain a leading platform.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller made the theoretical proposal; Blatt led key experimental demonstrations (entanglement of many ions, teleportation, quantum simulation). Wineland and Haroche were recognised in 2012 for ion and photon control, which partly overlaps experimentally and weakens the case for a further ion prize. The configuration is clean but overlaps with B038 and B044.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with multiple independent platforms (Innsbruck, NIST, Maryland, Quantinuum and others), though the quantum-computing technology is still developing and the ultimate impact is not settled.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2012 prize and with other candidates sharing Cirac and Zoller.
The most appropriate recognition might be shared with Wineland-group demonstrations not on the list.
Premature if the committee wants to see practical quantum advantage.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Prediction of the quantum spin Hall state and the Z2 topological insulator, followed by the observation in HgTe quantum wells, established a new class of materials with protected surface or edge states. This is among the most influential developments in condensed-matter physics of the century, with deep conceptual clarity.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the Z2 theory; Molenkamp led the HgTe experiment, building on the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang prediction, who are not on this list. Hasan's ARPES observation of the three-dimensional case is also pivotal. Any three-person selection leaves out key contributors (Zhang, Hasan, Fu, Moore, Balents), so allocation is a real obstacle.
assessment.maturity: Very mature and independently confirmed across materials and techniques; the field has produced extensive follow-on work and a recognised broader topological-matter programme.
uncertainties: Credit is split across theory, two-dimensional and three-dimensional experiments, with the absence of Zhang from the list.
Overlap with the Thouless-Haldane-Kosterlitz 2016 prize may lead some members to view it as already recognised.
The candidate partly overlaps with B025.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit quantum electrodynamics transferred cavity-QED concepts to superconducting circuits, enabling strong coupling, dispersive readout and the architecture of modern superconducting quantum processors. It is original and technologically consequential, and as an atomic physicist I appreciate the direct conceptual lineage from Haroche's cavity QED.
assessment.attribution: Blais, Wallraff and Schoelkopf (with Huard, Girvin and others in the original 2004 proposal and demonstration) are plausible but the 2004 papers have a larger author list. Allocation between theory and experiment is reasonable but not exhaustive.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed, but the 2025 prize already recognised macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits, so the committee may judge that the area has been recently honoured and that cQED should wait.
uncertainties: Recency of the 2025 prize on superconducting circuits.
Contributions of Girvin and others to the founding work.
Whether the committee wishes to recognise a platform whose commercial value is still unproven.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Programmable arrays of individually trapped Rydberg atoms use tweezers and Rydberg blockade to provide controllable many-body quantum systems for simulation and quantum computing. Techniques of atomic-structure control (long-lived Rydberg states, blockade, dipole interactions) are central, and the results (large-scale quantum simulation, logical qubits) are striking.
assessment.attribution: Zoller and Lukin contributed foundational theory (Rydberg gates with Jaksch, Lukin and collaborators); Browaeys, Lukin and Saffman demonstrated blockade and arrays; Bernien, Endres, Bloch's and other groups also contributed. Credit is diffuse and the list of four needs to be reduced.
assessment.maturity: Rapidly maturing but young; independent confirmation exists from several groups, though the long-term significance and a dominant architecture are not settled. Likely premature relative to the other candidates.
uncertainties: Prematurity and fast-moving field.
Overlap of Zoller and Lukin with other candidates.
Difficulty identifying a small set of decisive contributors.
